LINE PROJECT IN BELL, MCCULLOCH,                               §
CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASES,                                     §
LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH, MENARD,                               §
MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER,                            §       ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
TOM GREEN AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                              §


           MCCULLOCH COUNTY COMMISSIONER COURT’S INITIAL BRIEF

                   TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES

        NOW INTO COURT, through undersigned counsel, comes the McCulloch County Commissioners

Court (MCCC) who respectfully submits this Initial Brief in opposition to all routes and segments that run

through McCulloch County, Texas.

          I.       INTRODUCTION

        Beginning around June 2025, the MCCC began to hear concerns from its constituents regarding the

proposed 765kV transmission line project by Oncor Electric Delivery Company, LLC and LCRA

Transmission Services Company (“Applicants”). Understanding that McCulloch County is located in a part

of Texas that has remained relatively unchanged and thus a popular location for suburban and urban

visitors, and further understanding that the culture that permeates in rural Texas (and in McCulloch County

in particular) is one of the last few remaining, decent, authentic, and respectable attributes about this State,

the MCCC unanimously voted intervene and filed its Motion to Intervene on April 22, 2026.(PUC

Interchange—item 1184)

          II.      LEGAL STANDARD

        The MCCC intervened in this matter primarily in response to the differing realities of two different




                                                                                                              1
 laws. The first is HB 5066, passed in 2023 by the Texas Legislature, which enacted Texas Utilities Code

§§ 39.166 and 39.167. Public Utilities Commission staff witness John Pooled testified HB 5066 was the

“origin” of the proposed 765kV transmission line project when cross examined by McCulloch County

Attorney, Greg Torres. (SOAH Transcript—Hearing on the Merits—June 10, 2026-pg. 179 ). The second

is Texas Transportation Code § 251.003, giving county commissioners general responsibilities regarding

the maintenance of county roads. As will be discussed further, these laws together cannot be applied at the

same time.

        In addition, Under PURA §37.056(c), the Commission must consider several factors when

evaluating transmission line routes, including community values, recreational and park areas, historic

and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service.

          III.    APPLICATION

        Flooding & Road Concerns

        A common theme throughout the testimony from the MCCC and all the Intervenors in

McCulloch County is the concern over the conditions of the roads and the potential impact of future

flooding. Residents of McCulloch County saw firsthand the devastation of the “July 4th” 2025 floods

that wrecked parts of the Texas Hill Country—damaging roads in McCulloch County to an extent that

the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) had to get involved.

        How can the elected county commissioners maintain the county roads in McCulloch County

when they have not been properly restored?             According to McCulloch County Precinct 1

Commissioner Carol Anderson, some of these county roads span load limit bridges that are 75-100

years old.(PUC Interchange 59475—Item 3864) In short, the hauling of heavy equipment, construction

materials, and other traffic that would be associated with the construction of the proposed transmission

line would overwhelm already unreliable county roads. These are roads that counsel for MCCC

described as “undrivable” after a good rain—in a literal sense, and not hyperbole. Bad roads can inhibit

emergency management personnel and vehicles from being effective in life-or-death situations. During

cross examination, McCulloch County Precinct 2 Commissioner Randy Deans testified that he rescued


                                                                                                         2
 dozens of people during the July 4th, 2025, floods.

        Applicants appeared dismissive of these issues whenever they were raised during the

hearings—presenting as if these were mere inconveniences unworthy of 3-minute remarks. Despite

Applicants’ dismissive treatment of these issues, the proposed transmission line would jeopardize road

integrity and emergency management in McCulloch County, to the detriment of the citizens of

McCulloch County.

        Community Values

        In Texas nomenclature, McCulloch County is known as the “Heart of Texas” – a rural, agricultural

county in which the literal geographic center of Texas is located. McCulloch County citizens exemplify the

quintessential definition of what it means to be a Texan. McCulloch County is a community that is not

located on an interstate corridor, or within 100 miles of a major Texas city, and it is where central Texas,

the Texas Hill Country, and West Texas collide. It is a primarily agricultural county that attracts outdoor

enthusiasts, because it reminds people of what Texas used to be before greed and outside interests invaded

this state. McCulloch County’s rural, agricultural nature, as John Poole testified to during cross examination

by MCCC, is a “community value” under Texas Utilities Code §37.056(c). (SOAH Transcript-Hearing on

the Merits-June 10, 2026—Pg.179)

        As Texans, isn’t that worth preserving? A place where those that live there can enjoy the aspects

of rural living? And where those that have the money to do so can spend a nice weekend escaping the

concrete jungle of the urban Texas cities or cookie-cutter suburbs, perhaps by dressing in camouflage or

western wear and grabbing barbecue before heading out to dove hunt and then finish by watching football

in a cabin? Everybody in Texas likes that culture.

        However, understand there is a difference between rural recreation and rural living. MCCC opposes

all the proposed routes because it affects our day-to-day living. The residents of McCulloch County don’t

just exist in the county during Labor Day weekend or the first weekend of November; it is not merely a

community to visit occasionally for rural recreation, but rather where we live. Our way of life as rural

people—the values, culture, character, identity and history of McCulloch County—would be forever


                                                                                                            3
 changed if transmission line were to run through the county.

          IV.Other Route(s)

        As confirmed during cross examination of Applicants’ panel, there are proposed routes that do

not go through McCulloch County. (SOAH Transcript—Hearing on the Merits—June 9, 2026) MCCC

asks that one of the routes that does not traverse McCulloch County be chosen as the route for the

proposed transmission line. McCulloch County has residents who are affected by the transmission line

and did not receive notice of the proposed transmission line until early April 2026. Thus, they were

left with too little time to find an attorney before the hearing in this matter. Other affected properties

in McCulloch County are family legacy ranches whose owners have expressed opposition to the

proposed transmission line. Further, opting not to go through McCulloch County would avoid large

portions of the San Saba River. Lastly, McCulloch County would be negatively changed for

generations to come.

          V.       Conclusion

        There’s a country song, recorded originally by the Judds, titled “Grandpa Tell Me, ‘Bout the Good

Ol’ Days.” In it, there are lyrics that state “Everything is changing fast, they call it progress, but I just don’t

know.” That song is relatable to the matter at issue in this brief. It is not progress to inundate traditional

rural counties with battery storage facilities, data centers, wind turbines, solar farms, and yes, 765kV

transmission lines. It is not progress to ignore valid concerns from Texans for the sake of meeting a 180-

day timeline. It is not progress to destroy vulnerable county roads. It is certainly not progress to change the

character of an entire community. And no, potential tax revenue gained by the county because of the project

does not make it worth it, as was suggested by Applicants at the hearing on this matter. That mindset – in

short, choosing money over people – has contributed to Texas changing to something unrecognizable.

        Everything in Texas has changed. Our cities have become overtly political and unwelcoming. Our

suburbs are too expensive and have lost appeal. Our colleges and universities threw away over one hundred

years’ worth of rivalries and don’t even play in the same conference anymore. All accomplished for the




                                                                                                                 4
 sake of money. However, it is not too late to save rural Texas. McCulloch County can retain its identity and

way of life—forever the home of the true Heart of Texas.

        MCCC respectfully requests that the application for the proposed transmission line be denied.



                                                           Respectfully Submitted

                                                          Greg Torres

                                                          McCulloch County Attorney

                                                          105 N. Church St.

                                                          Brady, Texas 76825

                                                          (325) 597-9151

                                                          greg.torres@co.mcculloch.tx.us




                                                 By:

                                                                  Greg Torres

                                                                  State Bar No. 24097188

                                                                  McCulloch County Attorney
